course.title: Cooking Basics
course.tagline: Cook with confidence: knife skills, flavours and everyday meals that taste great.

days.title: Welcome to Your Kitchen
days.goal: Set up your kitchen, learn the rules of safety, and cook your first simple meal.

video.title: How To Master 5 Basic Cooking Skills

steps: Clear and wipe down your work surface and wash your hands for 20 seconds.
Find and lay out your basic tools: a sharp knife, chopping board, pot, pan and wooden spoon.
Learn the golden rule: wash hands after touching raw meat, and keep raw and cooked food apart.
Read a recipe all the way through before you start cooking.
Boil water, add a pinch of salt, and cook one egg for 7 minutes, then cool it in cold water.
days.task: Cook one boiled egg and peel it cleanly.
days.challenge: Time yourself: can you peel the egg in under one minute without tearing the white?

quiz.q: Why should you read a whole recipe before you start cooking?
options: To know the steps, tools and timing in advance
quiz.explain: Reading first stops surprises mid-cook, like missing ingredients or a step that needs an hour.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands?
quiz.explain: 20 seconds with soap removes most germs from your hands.

quiz.q: Where should raw meat be kept?
options: Away from cooked and ready-to-eat food
quiz.explain: Raw meat can drip juices carrying germs onto cooked food, so keep them apart.

days.title: Knife Skills: Hold, Grip and Cut Safely
days.goal: Hold a knife correctly and make safe, even cuts.

video.title: Learn the Absolute Basics of Cooking in This Crash Course

steps: Learn the pinch grip: thumb and forefinger pinching the blade just above the handle.
Curl your fingertips under (the claw) on the hand holding the food.
Place a damp cloth under your chopping board so it cannot slip.
Practise the rocking cut on an onion: steady, even slices, not sawing.
Cut a carrot into even batons about the same thickness so they cook evenly.
days.task: Slice one onion and one carrot into even pieces using the claw grip.
days.challenge: Cut the carrot batons so no two differ by more than a few millimetres.

quiz.q: What is the claw grip?
options: Holding the knife by the tip
Curling fingertips under so the knuckles guide the blade
Holding food with your palm flat
quiz.explain: Curled fingertips keep your fingers behind the blade; the knuckles guide the knife.

quiz.q: Why put a damp cloth under a chopping board?
quiz.explain: A slipping board is one of the commonest causes of knife cuts.

quiz.q: Why cut vegetables to even sizes?
options: So they cook at the same rate
quiz.explain: Uneven pieces cook unevenly: small ones burn while big ones stay raw.

days.title: How to Chop an Onion Without Tears
days.goal: Dice an onion quickly and cleanly.

video.title: How to Boil and Poach an Egg

steps: Peel the onion and cut it in half through the root.
Leave the root end on: it holds the layers together.
Make horizontal cuts toward the root, then vertical cuts, then slice across.
Keep the claw grip and let the knife do the work with a smooth rocking motion.
Sweep the diced onion into a bowl and rinse the board.
days.task: Dice two onions: one finely, one in larger chunks.
days.challenge: Chill the onion in the fridge for 15 minutes first and see if your eyes water less.

quiz.q: Why leave the root end on when dicing an onion?
options: It holds the layers together while you cut
quiz.explain: The root holds the layers in place so your cuts stay neat.

quiz.q: What order of cuts gives a dice?
quiz.explain: Horizontal then vertical cuts, finished by slicing across, make even dice.

quiz.q: What really causes onion tears?
options: Sulfur compounds released when cells are cut
quiz.explain: Cutting releases sulfur compounds that irritate the eyes; a sharp knife and cold onion reduce them.

days.title: Garlic and Herbs: Small Cuts, Big Flavour
days.goal: Chop garlic and fresh herbs without bruising them.

video.title: How to Peel and Cut an Avocado

steps: Peel garlic by smashing the clove lightly with the flat of your knife.
Mince garlic with a rocking motion, scraping the pile back together as you go.
Pick herb leaves off woody stems; keep soft stems of parsley and coriander.
Chop herbs with a sharp knife in a few strokes; do not grind them back and forth.
Store leftover chopped herbs in a little oil in a sealed container.
days.task: Mince 4 garlic cloves and chop a small bunch of parsley.
days.challenge: Mince the garlic in under 2 minutes with no large chunks left.

quiz.q: How do you peel a garlic clove fast?
options: Smash it lightly with the flat of the knife
quiz.explain: A light smash loosens the skin so it slips off.

quiz.q: Why should you not over-chop fresh herbs?
options: Bruising releases bitter flavours and darkens them
quiz.explain: Too much chopping bruises herbs, turning them dark and bitter.

quiz.q: When should garlic go into a hot pan?
options: After the onion has softened, so it does not burn
quiz.explain: Garlic burns in under a minute; add it after the onion softens.

days.title: Boiling, Simmering and Steaming
days.goal: Control heat and water to boil and simmer properly.
steps: Learn the difference: a boil is big rolling bubbles, a simmer is small gentle bubbles.
Salt pasta water so it tastes like the sea, about 1 tablespoon per litre.
Boil an egg: 6 minutes for jammy, 10 for fully set; cool in cold water.
Simmer a simple tomato sauce on low for 15 minutes with the lid half on.
Steam vegetables in a colander over boiling water for 3 to 5 minutes.
days.task: Boil eggs two ways (6 minutes and 10 minutes) and compare the yolks.
days.challenge: Steam broccoli so it stays bright green and still has a bite.

quiz.q: What is the difference between boiling and simmering?
options: Boiling is rolling bubbles, simmering is gentle small bubbles
quiz.explain: A boil is vigorous; a simmer is gentle heat just below boiling.

quiz.q: Why salt pasta water?
options: To season the pasta from the inside
quiz.explain: Salted water seasons the pasta itself, which sauce alone cannot do.

quiz.q: Why cool boiled eggs in cold water?
options: To make them peel easier and stop the yolk greying
quiz.explain: Cold water stops the cooking and shrinks the egg slightly from the shell, so it peels cleanly.

days.title: Rice, Perfect Every Time
days.goal: Cook fluffy, separate-grained rice on the stove.
steps: Rinse rice in cold water until the water runs mostly clear.
Use the ratio: 1 part rice to 1.5 parts water for long-grain white rice.
Bring to a boil, then drop to the lowest heat, cover, and do not lift the lid.
Cook 12 to 15 minutes, then rest off the heat for 10 minutes, lid still on.
Fluff gently with a fork, never stir while it cooks.
days.task: Cook a pot of white rice with no sticking and no mush.
days.challenge: Cook the rice again tomorrow using the finger measure (water one knuckle above the rice) and compare.

quiz.q: Why rinse rice before cooking?
options: To remove surface starch so grains stay separate
quiz.explain: Excess starch makes rice sticky and clumpy.

quiz.q: Why must you not lift the lid while rice cooks?
options: It lets steam escape and ruins the timing
It cools the pot too much only
quiz.explain: Rice cooks in trapped steam; lifting the lid lets it out and leaves the top undercooked.

quiz.q: Why rest rice for 10 minutes after cooking?
options: So the steam finishes cooking and the grains firm up
quiz.explain: Resting lets moisture even out so the rice is fluffy, not wet.

days.title: Week 1 Project: Your First Full Meal
days.goal: Cook a complete simple meal from scratch using this week's skills.
steps: Plan a meal: rice, a protein, and a vegetable side.
Write a shopping list and a cooking order, starting with the slowest item.
Prep everything first: chop onions, garlic and herbs before any heat goes on.
Cook the rice, then the protein, then the vegetables, timing them to finish together.
Plate it neatly, taste, season, and serve.
days.task: Cook a full meal for yourself or your household today.
days.challenge: Cook the same meal again but finish everything within 45 minutes.

quiz.q: What does 'mise en place' mean?
options: Everything in its place: prep before you cook
quiz.explain: Prepping and measuring everything first makes cooking calm and on time.

quiz.q: What should you cook first in a multi-dish meal?
options: The slowest dish, so all finish together
quiz.explain: Start with what takes longest so everything lands on the table at once.

quiz.q: Why taste and season at the end?
options: Flavours concentrate as food cooks, so final seasoning is most accurate
quiz.explain: Sauces reduce and flavours build, so the final taste is the true one.

project.title: Cook a Complete Meal
project.brief: Plan and cook a full meal: rice, a protein and a vegetable side, served at one time.
checks: Meal planned with a shopping list and cooking order
Onions, garlic and herbs chopped safely with the claw grip
Rice cooked fluffy and separate, not sticky
Protein cooked through and seasoned
Vegetables cooked, not overdone
Everything served together, hot, and plated neatly

days.title: Frying: Shallow, Deep and Stir-Fry
days.goal: Fry food safely and get crisp, golden results.
steps: Heat oil until it shimmers; test with a small piece of food: it should sizzle at once.
Pat food dry before frying so oil does not spit.
Do not crowd the pan: cook in batches so the temperature stays high.
Turn food once, not constantly, so a crust can form.
Drain fried food on a wire rack or paper towel, and season while hot.
days.task: Shallow-fry plantain or chicken pieces until golden.
days.challenge: Fry a second batch without crowding and compare the crispness.

quiz.q: Why pat food dry before frying?
options: Water in hot oil spits and drops the temperature
quiz.explain: Water turns to steam violently in hot oil and cools the oil, making food soggy.

quiz.q: Why not crowd the pan?
options: The oil temperature drops and food steams instead of frying
quiz.explain: Crowding drops the oil temperature, so food goes soggy instead of crisp.

quiz.q: Why season fried food while it is hot?
options: Salt sticks better to hot, slightly oily surfaces
quiz.explain: Salt clings to the hot surface; once food cools and dries, salt falls off.

days.title: How to Cook Pasta Properly
days.goal: Cook pasta al dente and pair it with a simple sauce.
steps: Use a large pot with plenty of salted water.
Add pasta only when the water is at a full rolling boil.
Stir in the first minute so it does not stick together.
Taste a piece 1 minute before the packet time: it should be firm, not soft.
Save a cup of pasta water to loosen and bind the sauce.
days.task: Cook spaghetti and toss it in a quick garlic and tomato sauce.
days.challenge: Cook the pasta so it finishes in the sauce, not in the water.

quiz.q: When should pasta go into the pot?
options: When the water is at a full rolling boil
quiz.explain: Boiling water sets the surface starch quickly so pasta does not clump.

quiz.q: What does 'al dente' mean?
quiz.explain: Al dente means firm to the bite, the correct texture for pasta.

quiz.q: Why save pasta water?
options: Its starch helps the sauce cling and thicken
quiz.explain: Starchy pasta water helps the sauce stick to the pasta instead of sliding off.

days.title: Roasting Chicken and Vegetables
days.goal: Roast a whole chicken with vegetables in one tray.

video.title: How to Make a Baked Potato

steps: Pat the chicken dry and season inside and out with salt, pepper and garlic.
Cut vegetables into similar sizes and toss in oil and salt.
Roast at 200°C, chicken on top of the vegetables so the juices drip down.
Cook until the juices run clear and the thickest part reaches 75°C.
Rest the chicken 10 minutes before carving so the juices stay in.
days.task: Roast a whole chicken with potatoes and carrots.
days.challenge: Carve the chicken neatly into 8 pieces.

quiz.q: Why rest roast chicken before carving?
options: Juices redistribute so the meat stays moist
quiz.explain: Cutting at once lets the juices run out; resting keeps them in the meat.

quiz.q: What temperature must chicken reach inside?
quiz.explain: 75°C kills harmful bacteria in poultry.

quiz.q: Why put vegetables under the chicken?
options: Chicken juices drip down and flavour them
quiz.explain: The drippings baste the vegetables with flavour.

days.title: Soups and Stews: Building Flavour
days.goal: Build a soup or stew in layers of flavour.

video.title: How to Cook Roast Chicken and Vegetables

steps: Start with onion, garlic and a little oil: the flavour base.
Brown meat or vegetables first for deeper colour and taste.
Add liquid, bring to a boil, then simmer low and slow.
Season in stages and taste at the end.
Skim any foam or fat from the surface while it simmers.
days.task: Make a simple vegetable or chicken soup from scratch.
days.challenge: Make the same soup with one extra spice and note the difference.

quiz.q: Why brown meat before adding liquid?
quiz.explain: Browning makes deep, rich flavours that water alone cannot make.

quiz.q: Why simmer a stew low and slow?
options: Tough fibres soften and flavours meld
quiz.explain: Gentle long cooking breaks down tough meat and blends flavours.

quiz.q: Why season in stages?
options: Flavours build as food cooks, so you adjust as you go
quiz.explain: Seasoning in stages builds depth; one big dose at the end tastes flat.

days.title: Eggs: Fried, Scrambled and Omelette
days.goal: Cook eggs three ways with confidence.

video.title: The Most Essential Knife Skills You Need For Everyday Cooking

steps: Fried egg: medium heat, a little oil, lid on for 1 minute to set the top.
Scrambled: low heat, constant slow stirring, take off the heat while still slightly runny.
Omelette: whisk eggs with salt, pour into a hot buttered pan, fill and fold.
Use fresh eggs: they hold their shape better in the pan.
Season eggs after cooking, not before, for a better texture.
days.task: Cook one fried egg, one scrambled egg and one omelette.
days.challenge: Make an omelette with a filling of your choice, folded without tearing.

quiz.q: Why cook scrambled eggs on low heat?
options: High heat makes them rubbery and dry
quiz.explain: Gentle heat and slow stirring give soft, creamy curds.

quiz.q: Why take scrambled eggs off the heat while still slightly runny?
quiz.explain: The eggs keep cooking in their own heat, so stopping early stops them going dry.

quiz.q: How do you know an egg is fresh?
options: It sinks and lies flat in water
quiz.explain: Fresh eggs sink and lie flat; old eggs float because air builds up inside.

days.title: Seasoning and Tasting Like a Cook
days.goal: Season food with salt, acid, heat and sweetness in balance.
steps: Taste as you cook, not only at the end.
Salt in small pinches and taste after each one.
Add acid (lemon, lime or vinegar) to brighten rich or fatty food.
Add a pinch of sugar or honey to balance tomato or chilli heat.
Write down what worked so you can repeat it.
days.task: Take a plain soup and adjust it with salt, then lemon, then a pinch of sugar, tasting each step.
days.challenge: Fix an over-salted soup using potato or extra water and record what worked.

quiz.q: What does acid like lemon do in a dish?
options: Brightens and balances rich, fatty flavours
quiz.explain: Acid cuts through richness and lifts the other flavours.

quiz.q: What balances too much chilli heat?
quiz.explain: Sugar or dairy softens heat; water spreads it around.

quiz.q: Why season in small pinches?
options: You can always add more, but you cannot take it out
quiz.explain: Over-salting is hard to fix, so build up slowly.

days.title: Week 2 Project: Cook for Two
days.goal: Plan and cook a two-course meal for two people.
steps: Choose a starter and a main that share ingredients to save money.
Write a timeline working backwards from serving time.
Prep all vegetables and seasonings before cooking anything.
Cook the main first if it needs resting, then the starter.
Serve both courses, ask for honest feedback, and note it down.
days.task: Cook a two-course meal for two people.
days.challenge: Serve the meal with a drink you made yourself, like fresh juice or zobo.

quiz.q: Why work backwards from serving time?
options: It makes sure every dish is ready at the right moment
quiz.explain: A backwards timeline stops dishes finishing too early or too late.

quiz.q: Why share ingredients between courses?
options: To save money and reduce waste
quiz.explain: Shared ingredients cut cost and waste.

quiz.q: What is the best way to get useful feedback?
options: Ask what they liked and what they would change
quiz.explain: Specific questions give answers you can actually cook better with.

project.title: Cook a Two-Course Meal for Two
project.brief: Cook a starter and a main for two people, served on time and on budget.
checks: Two courses planned with a shared-ingredients list
Timeline written backwards from serving time
Both dishes seasoned and tasted before serving
Main course rested if needed and served hot
Starter and main served in order, without a long wait
Feedback collected and written down

days.title: Baked Potatoes and Simple Sides
days.goal: Make baked potatoes and two quick sides.
steps: Scrub potatoes, prick with a fork, rub with oil and salt.
Bake at 200°C for about an hour until the skin is crisp and the inside is fluffy.
Make a quick side salad: wash, dry and chop leaves, add a simple oil and lemon dressing.
Steam green beans for 3 minutes, then toss with garlic butter.
Serve sides that contrast: one hot, one cold, one crunchy.
days.task: Bake potatoes and serve with a salad and garlic green beans.
days.challenge: Try a stuffed baked potato with a filling of your choice.

quiz.q: Why prick a potato before baking?
options: So steam escapes and it does not burst
quiz.explain: Steam builds inside a sealed potato and can make it burst.

quiz.q: Why dry salad leaves before dressing?
quiz.explain: Wet leaves repel dressing, so the salad tastes watery.

quiz.q: How long should green beans steam?
options: About 3 minutes, so they stay crisp
quiz.explain: Three minutes keeps beans bright and crisp; longer makes them limp.

days.title: Stir-Fry: Fast, Hot and Fresh
days.goal: Stir-fry vegetables and chicken in minutes.

video.title: Kelvin's Easy Kitchen Basics | Learn Cooking Step by Step Before Culinary School

steps: Cut everything into similar small sizes before heating the pan.
Get the pan very hot and add oil just before the food.
Cook in small batches so food fries instead of steaming.
Add sauce at the end and toss for 30 seconds.
Serve immediately over rice or noodles.
days.task: Make a chicken and vegetable stir-fry.
days.challenge: Stir-fry again using only vegetables and compare the timing.

quiz.q: Why must stir-fry ingredients be cut before the pan heats?
options: Stir-frying is so fast there is no time to chop mid-cook
quiz.explain: A stir-fry takes minutes; if you stop to chop, the food in the pan burns.

quiz.q: Why cook stir-fry in small batches?
options: A crowded pan steams food instead of frying it
quiz.explain: Too much food drops the pan temperature and the food goes soggy.

quiz.q: When does sauce go into a stir-fry?
options: At the end, tossed for 30 seconds
quiz.explain: Sauce added early burns or makes everything soggy; added last it coats and glazes.

days.title: Chicken Fried Rice from Scratch
days.goal: Make chicken fried rice with day-old rice.

video.title: Learn the Absolute Basics of Cooking in This Crash Course

steps: Use cold, day-old rice: fresh rice turns mushy in the pan.
Scramble the egg first, remove it, then fry the chicken.
Add onion, garlic and vegetables, then the rice.
Season with soy sauce, a little salt and pepper.
Toss everything on high heat for 2 minutes, then add the egg back.
days.task: Cook chicken fried rice for your household.
days.challenge: Make a second version with different vegetables and note the best combo.

quiz.q: Why use day-old rice for fried rice?
options: Cold, dry rice fries into separate grains instead of mush
quiz.explain: Fresh rice is too moist and clumps; cold rice stays separate.

quiz.q: Why scramble the egg first and set it aside?
options: So it does not overcook while the rest fries
quiz.explain: Egg cooks in seconds; adding it back at the end keeps it tender.

quiz.q: What does soy sauce add besides salt?
quiz.explain: Soy sauce adds a deep savoury taste and a golden colour.

days.title: Sauces: The Five You Will Use Most
days.goal: Make a simple tomato sauce, a white sauce, a gravy, a stir-fry sauce and a dressing.

video.title: How to Boil and Poach an Egg

steps: Tomato sauce: onion, garlic, tomatoes, simmer 20 minutes.
White sauce: melt butter, stir in flour, add milk slowly, stir until thick.
Gravy: use roast pan juices, add flour, then stock, and simmer.
Stir-fry sauce: soy sauce, honey, garlic and a little water.
Dressing: 3 parts oil to 1 part lemon juice or vinegar, with salt.
days.task: Make two sauces today and use them on a meal.
days.challenge: Store the leftover sauce in a sealed container and label it with the date.

quiz.q: What is the flour-and-butter base of a white sauce called?
quiz.explain: A roux is equal parts butter and flour cooked together, the base of white sauce.

quiz.q: Why add milk slowly to a roux?
quiz.explain: Adding liquid slowly while stirring stops lumps forming.

quiz.q: What is the classic oil-to-acid ratio for a dressing?
quiz.explain: Three parts oil to one part acid gives a balanced dressing.

days.title: Cooking on a Budget: Plan the Week
days.goal: Plan a week of meals that wastes nothing.

video.title: How to Peel and Cut an Avocado

steps: List what you already have in the cupboard and fridge.
Plan meals around one or two cheap proteins, like eggs, beans or chicken.
Cook once, eat twice: make extra rice or stew and use it the next day.
Use leftovers in a new dish, like fried rice or a wrap.
Cost each meal and keep the week under your budget.
days.task: Write a 7-day meal plan using what you already have plus one shop.
days.challenge: Cost your plan and cut it by 10 percent without losing a meal.

quiz.q: What does 'cook once, eat twice' mean?
options: Cook double and eat it all
Make extra and reuse it in another meal
quiz.explain: Cooking extra and reusing it saves time, gas and money.

quiz.q: What is the first step in budget meal planning?
quiz.explain: Knowing what you have stops you buying things twice.

quiz.q: Why plan meals around one or two proteins?
options: Buying in bulk is cheaper and simpler
quiz.explain: Fewer proteins bought in larger amounts cost less per meal.

days.title: Kitchen Safety and First Aid
days.goal: Prevent the commonest kitchen injuries and handle them calmly.
steps: Keep pan handles turned in so they cannot be knocked.
Never put water on a grease fire: smother it with a lid or damp cloth.
Keep knives sharp: a dull knife slips and cuts worse.
For a small burn, run cool water over it for 10 minutes.
Know where your first aid kit is and keep a phone nearby.
days.task: Do a safety check of your kitchen and fix three hazards.
days.challenge: Practise the grease-fire rule: lid on, heat off, never water.

quiz.q: What should you never do to a grease fire?
quiz.explain: Water turns to steam and throws burning oil everywhere.

quiz.q: Why is a dull knife more dangerous than a sharp one?
options: It slips off food and cuts you
quiz.explain: A dull blade needs more force and slips, which causes deep cuts.

quiz.q: How long should you run cool water on a small burn?
quiz.explain: Ten minutes of cool running water cools the burn properly.

days.title: Week 3 Project: Three Dishes, One Table
days.goal: Cook three different dishes and serve them together as a spread.
steps: Pick three dishes that use different methods: one fried, one boiled or stewed, one roasted.
Write a full shopping list and a cooking timeline.
Prep everything first, then cook in order of longest to shortest.
Keep finished dishes warm in a low oven while you finish the rest.
Serve all three at once, with a drink, and photograph the table.
days.task: Cook a three-dish spread for your household.
days.challenge: Serve the same spread to a guest and ask for their favourite dish.

quiz.q: Why use different cooking methods in one spread?
options: Different methods give different textures and flavours
quiz.explain: A mix of fried, stewed and roasted food gives variety on the table.

quiz.q: How do you keep finished dishes warm?
quiz.explain: A low oven keeps food warm without overcooking it.

quiz.q: What is the best order to cook three dishes?
options: Longest first, so all finish together
quiz.explain: Starting with the slowest dish means everything is ready at the same time.

project.title: Cook a Three-Dish Spread
project.brief: Cook three dishes using different methods and serve them together.
checks: Three dishes chosen using different cooking methods
Shopping list and timeline written
All prep done before cooking starts
Each dish seasoned and cooked properly
Dishes served together, warm, with a drink
Table photographed and feedback noted

days.title: Freezing and Storing Leftovers
days.goal: Store cooked food safely and reheat it well.
steps: Cool cooked food quickly in shallow containers, within 2 hours.
Label containers with the dish name and the date.
Freeze in flat bags or small portions so they thaw fast.
Thaw in the fridge overnight, never on the counter.
Reheat until steaming hot all the way through, 75°C.
days.task: Cook extra stew, cool it, label it and freeze two portions.
days.challenge: Thaw one portion in the fridge and reheat it properly the next day.

quiz.q: How fast must cooked food be cooled and stored?
quiz.explain: Food left out over 2 hours sits in the danger zone where bacteria grow fast.

quiz.q: Why freeze in flat bags?
quiz.explain: Flat portions freeze and thaw quickly and evenly.

quiz.q: What temperature must reheated food reach?
quiz.explain: Reheating to 75°C all the way through kills bacteria.

days.title: Cooking for Guests: Portions and Timing
days.goal: Scale recipes up and serve guests without stress.
steps: Multiply a recipe by the number of guests, keeping the ratios the same.
Add about 10 percent extra for big eaters and seconds.
Use a bigger pot, not a fuller one: food needs room to cook.
Set the table before you start cooking.
Serve in courses or family style so nobody waits hungry.
days.task: Cook a meal for 4 or more people, scaling a recipe you already know.
days.challenge: Time the meal from first prep to serving and write the real time down.

quiz.q: When scaling a recipe up, what stays the same?
quiz.explain: Doubling a recipe means doubling every ingredient to keep the balance.

quiz.q: Why add about 10 percent extra?
quiz.explain: A small buffer stops you running out when guests eat more.

quiz.q: Why use a bigger pot when cooking more?
options: Food needs space to cook evenly
quiz.explain: An overfull pot steams instead of frying and cooks unevenly.

days.title: Baking Basics: Your First Bread
days.goal: Bake a simple loaf of bread from scratch.
steps: Mix flour, yeast, salt and warm water into a soft dough.
Knead for 10 minutes until smooth and springy.
Cover and leave to rise for 1 hour until doubled in size.
Shape into a loaf, rest 30 minutes, then bake at 200°C for 25 to 30 minutes.
Cool on a rack before slicing so the inside sets.
days.task: Bake one loaf of bread.
days.challenge: Bake a second loaf with herbs or garlic mixed into the dough.

quiz.q: Why knead bread dough?
options: To build gluten so the bread rises and holds shape
quiz.explain: Kneading develops gluten, the stretchy network that traps gas and makes bread rise.

quiz.q: Why leave dough to rise?
options: So yeast makes gas and the dough doubles
quiz.explain: Yeast feeds on sugars and releases gas, which makes the dough rise.

quiz.q: Why cool bread before slicing?
options: The inside is still setting; cutting early makes it gummy
It is too hot to hold
quiz.explain: Hot bread is still cooking inside; slicing early gives a doughy, gummy crumb.

days.title: One-Pot Meals: Less Washing, More Flavour
days.goal: Cook complete meals in a single pot.

video.title: How to Make a Baked Potato

steps: Brown the protein first, then remove it and cook the onions in the same pot.
Add rice or pasta, liquid and seasonings, then return the protein.
Keep the lid on and cook on low until the grains are done.
Stir once or twice only, so the bottom does not stick.
Rest 5 minutes, then serve straight from the pot.
days.task: Cook a one-pot chicken and rice dish.
days.challenge: Cook a one-pot pasta dish and compare the washing up.

quiz.q: Why brown the protein first in a one-pot meal?
options: Browning adds flavour that stays in the pot
quiz.explain: The browned bits left in the pot flavour everything that cooks after.

quiz.q: Why stir a one-pot rice dish only once or twice?
options: Too much stirring makes rice sticky and breaks it
quiz.explain: Over-stirring releases starch and turns rice gluey.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of one-pot cooking?
options: Fewer dishes and flavours that build in one pot
quiz.explain: One pot means less washing and flavours layering in the same pot.

days.title: Breakfast Like a Cook
days.goal: Cook a proper breakfast spread in 30 minutes.

video.title: How to Cook Roast Chicken and Vegetables

steps: Start with the slowest item: boiled or baked potatoes.
Cook eggs last, since they take minutes.
Fry plantain or make pancakes while the eggs cook.
Make a quick fruit salad with whatever fruit you have.
Serve everything hot at once with tea or coffee.
days.task: Cook a full breakfast: eggs, plantain or pancakes, and fruit.
days.challenge: Time the breakfast and try to finish everything in 30 minutes.

quiz.q: What should you cook first at breakfast?
quiz.explain: Slow items start first so everything finishes together.

quiz.q: Why cook eggs last?
options: They cook in minutes and go cold fast
quiz.explain: Eggs cook in 2 to 3 minutes and cool quickly, so they go last.

quiz.q: What makes a good breakfast spread?
options: A mix of hot, fresh and sweet items
quiz.explain: A mix of hot food, fresh fruit and a drink makes a balanced breakfast.

days.title: Taste, Adjust, Serve: The Cook's Final Check
days.goal: Do a final taste-and-adjust pass on any dish.

video.title: The Most Essential Knife Skills You Need For Everyday Cooking

steps: Taste with a clean spoon, not your fingers.
Ask: does it need salt, acid, heat or sweetness?
Adjust one thing at a time and taste again.
Check the temperature: hot food should be hot, cold food cold.
Garnish simply: fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon.
days.task: Take yesterday's leftovers and improve them with one adjustment.
days.challenge: Cook a dish, then deliberately fix it three ways and record the best.

quiz.q: Why taste with a clean spoon?
options: It avoids spreading germs from your mouth
quiz.explain: Double-dipping spreads germs into the food.

quiz.q: Why adjust only one thing at a time?
options: So you know what fixed it
quiz.explain: Changing one thing at a time tells you exactly what worked.

quiz.q: What is a garnish for?
options: To add colour, freshness or a final flavour lift
quiz.explain: A simple garnish adds colour and a last touch of flavour.

days.title: Your Signature Dish
days.goal: Choose and perfect one dish you can cook brilliantly.
steps: Pick a dish you love and have cooked at least twice.
Write the recipe in your own words with exact amounts.
Cook it again, timing every step and noting problems.
Fix the problems: adjust seasoning, timing or method.
Cook it once more until it is consistent every time.
days.task: Cook your chosen signature dish and write the final recipe down.
days.challenge: Cook your signature dish for someone else and get their verdict.

quiz.q: What makes a dish a 'signature dish'?
options: A dish you can cook brilliantly and consistently
A dish with a fancy name
quiz.explain: A signature dish is one you have mastered and can repeat with the same great result.

quiz.q: Why write the recipe in your own words?
options: So you understand it and can repeat it
quiz.explain: Writing it yourself forces you to understand each step.

quiz.q: Why cook the same dish several times?
quiz.explain: Repeating a dish reveals the problems and locks in the good result.

days.title: Revision Week: Skills Check
days.goal: Revisit the core skills from the whole course.
steps: Re-practise knife skills: dice an onion and mince garlic.
Cook rice and a sauce from memory, without the recipe.
Name the five heat methods: boiling, frying, roasting, steaming, grilling.
Check your food safety habits: hand washing, storage, reheating.
List your three strongest skills and one you still want to improve.
days.task: Cook a full meal from memory, using no recipe at all.
days.challenge: Ask someone to watch you cook and point out one safety habit to fix.

quiz.q: What are the five basic heat methods?
quiz.explain: Boiling, frying, roasting, steaming and grilling are the core ways to apply heat.

quiz.q: Why cook a meal from memory?
options: It proves you really know the steps
quiz.explain: Cooking without a recipe shows the skills are truly learned.

quiz.q: What should you do with a skill you still find weak?
options: Practise it on purpose until it improves
quiz.explain: Deliberate practice on weak spots is how a cook keeps growing.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your Final Cook
days.goal: Plan your capstone meal and gather everything you need.
steps: Choose your capstone menu: a starter, a main and a side.
Write the full shopping list with costs.
Write the cooking timeline, working backwards from serving.
Check you have every tool and ingredient ready.
Cook a trial run of the hardest dish if you have time.
days.task: Write your complete capstone plan and share it with a friend for feedback.
days.challenge: Do a trial run of your capstone main dish today.

quiz.q: What should your capstone menu show?
options: Everything you learned: knife skills, heat control, seasoning and timing
quiz.explain: The capstone proves the whole course: prep, cooking methods, seasoning and timing.

quiz.q: Why do a trial run of the hardest dish?
options: To find problems before the real cook
quiz.explain: A trial run finds timing or seasoning problems while there is still time to fix them.

quiz.q: Why work backwards from serving time?
options: So every dish is ready at the same moment
quiz.explain: A backwards timeline is how cooks land a whole meal on the table hot.

capstone.title: The Confident Cook's Final Meal
capstone.brief: Cook a complete three-part meal from scratch for your household or guests: a starter, a main with rice or potatoes, and a side. Use the knife skills, heat control, seasoning and timing you learned across the 30 days, and serve everything hot at the same time.
checks: Menu planned with a shopping list and a backwards timeline
Onions, garlic and herbs prepped safely with correct knife technique
Rice or potatoes cooked properly, not sticky or raw
Main dish seasoned, cooked through and tasty
Starter and side served with the main, all hot at once
Kitchen left clean and food stored safely afterwards
Feedback collected from at least one person who ate the meal
deliverables: A photo of the finished meal on the table
Your written menu with the shopping list and costs
Your cooking timeline, working backwards from serving time
Your signature dish recipe written in your own words
A short note on what you learned and what you will improve next
